title: Model catalog — health snapshot & selection storyline
audience: Product marketing, growth, solutions engineering, docs
summary: Working draft: recommended narrative and tactical notes for positioning the Model Catalog around measurable model health, selection guidance for customers, and a lightweight assurance/badge system for open models. Focus: make tradeoffs explicit (cost vs. quality), reduce friction in selection, and create defensible GTM messages against managed model APIs.
content:
Problem statement and goal:

Many customers are confused by the breadth of open models: similar names, inconsistent metric reporting, and hidden tradeoffs (latency, prompt sensitivity, quantization artifacts). Our goal is to give developers clear, comparable signals so they can pick the right model quickly and trust Redwood’s catalog recommendations. We want a narrative that emphasizes engineering-first tradeoffs and measurability rather than marketing claims.

Core positioning thesis (one-liner):
Make the model decision a measurement problem, not a guessing game—Redwood’s catalog surfaces model health and workload fit so teams can choose with predictable latency, cost, and quality.

Key concepts to introduce (simple language for docs and website):
- Health Snapshot: short, standardized summary of a model’s critical serving properties (latency P50/P95 at common sequence lengths, median throughput on instance class, KV-cache friendliness, memory headroom).
- Assurance Badges: small, policy-based flags (not endorsements) that indicate a model passes specific guardrails we run (e.g., "Continuous Batching Friendly", "Quant-ready", "OpenWeights-Audited").
- Evaluation Signals: numeric scores from our standard eval suites broken down by workload (summarization, instruction-following, code, hallucination rate on adversarial prompts).
- Cost/Quality Tradeoff Bands: visual bands that place models across three axes — cost per token, tail latency, and task-specific quality — so customers can prioritize.

Why this is different (competitive angle):
- Opponents focus on model brand or raw capability claims. Redwood focuses on serving-fit and economics: we quantify how a model will behave in production across deployment modes.
- We turn runtime characteristics (not just bench GPT scores) into first-class placement criteria. That matters for engineering teams choosing between hosted, dedicated, or private.

Suggested product copy snippets (for catalog cards, docs, and quickstart):
- Short (catalog card): "Health Snapshot: p50 18ms @128 tokens • p95 120ms @512 • Cost band: low | Task: instruction, summarization"
- One-liner: "Choose a model that fits your SLAs — we surface real serving metrics, eval signals, and cost bands so you can ship with predictable economics."
- Elevator pitch for PMM/AE: "Instead of asking 'is X model better than Y?', ask 'which model meets my latency, cost, and safety needs?' Redwood’s catalog gives the answer with measured signals and easy filters."

Concrete metrics to publish per model (minimum viable set):
- Latency: P50 and P95 at 128, 256, 512 token scenarios on our hosted instance class (and a note for dedicated sizing).
- Throughput: tokens/sec for small-batch (1) and batch-optimized (8) workloads.
- Memory: typical vram footprint (fp16/quant) and recommended instance family.
- Quantization compatibility: supported quant formats (8-bit, 4-bit) and expected quality delta (mean eval score drop).
- Eval suite breakdown: scores for NLU, summarization, instruction-following, hallucination rate on adversarial set.
- Security-review flags: whether the upstream weights have a license or encoder that raises risk, and whether we performed weight-audit steps.

Assurance Badge taxonomy (suggested names and semantics):
- Continuous-Batching-Friendly (CBF): model retains correctness under our batching strategy (low instability in chat sessions).
- Quant-Resilient: minimal quality degradation under our recommended quant settings.
- Latency-Optimized: P95 within target on standard instance class.
- Open-Weights-Audited: we checked license and basic supply-chain metadata for the published weights.
- Safety-Scoped: passed our automated safety filters for the evaluated domains (not a guarantee of safety for all prompts).

Badge UI guidance (catalog):
- Badges are informational toggles; they are not endorsements. Each badge links to a short explainer page that lists what tests we ran, thresholds, and caveats.
- Don’t show badges if a model is missing required data; show "Data incomplete" CTA to request a health snapshot.

Competitive notes (quick bullets):
- Managed LLM APIs (big providers): Strengths — turnkey, consistent SLA; Weakness — opaque runtime economics, limited visibility into model internals. Our counter: show precise serving metrics and predictable cost bands, and position as the developer-friendly alternative with better transparency.
- Open-source communities / model hubs: Strengths — breadth of models and deep research context; Weakness — inconsistent serving guidance. Our counter: curate and standardize signals and surface actionable selection guidance for production.
- Specialized inference vendors: Strengths — extreme optimizations for particular models; Weakness — narrower model coverage and less integrated policy tooling. Our counter: broad model catalog + runtime-aware routing and badging.

Suggested product flows (short):
1) Quick filter: Customer chooses baseline constraints (max P95 latency, max cost per 1k tokens, task type). Catalog returns ranked models with health snapshots.
2) Workload probe: Customer runs a lightweight "probe" with 5 canonical prompts in our hosted sandbox; we return a per-model probe report (latency, token cost, sample outputs).
3) Pin & stage: From probe results, customer pins model version to a route and selects rollout policy (canary + fallback to cost-tier model).

Tactical recommendations for launch (MVP -> v1):
- MVP: publish Health Snapshot with latency/throughput and eval suite scores + two badges (Latency-Optimized, Open-Weights-Audited). Add quick filters on the catalog UI and a short docs page explaining how to interpret numbers.
- v1: Add Workload Probes, more badges (Quant-Resilient, CBF), and per-route costing calculator. Integrate signals into Redwood Console routing suggestions (e.g., suggest a cheaper quantized variant for background tasks).
- Content: blog post "How we measure model health for production" with a reproducible mini-benchmark and repo link. Case study: internal cost-savings example for a customer who switched to a quant-resilient variant.

Common objections and suggested responses (AE / PMM crib notes):
- Objection: "These badges seem subjective." Response: "We explicitly publish test suites, thresholds, and raw metrics. Badges are deterministic outputs of tests you can reproduce."
- Objection: "Open models are risky for compliance." Response: "We surface license/metadata, run a lightweight weight-audit, and provide Private deployment options for customers who need full control."
- Objection: "How do I trust your latency numbers vs my infra?" Response: "We provide standardized numbers on our hosted instance class and a small sizing guide for Dedicated/Private so you can extrapolate. We also offer a 5-probe sandbox run to get live numbers on your traffic shape."

Measurement plan for adoption (OKRs):
- OKR 1: 40% of new catalog visitors use the quick filter within 6 months of launch.
- OKR 2: Reduction in model-related PoC time: 30% fewer customers open support tickets about model selection.
- OKR 3: 20% of route rollouts use a probe-run before pinning in the first year.

Open questions and risks (for product and legal):
- Do we need strict language for "Open-Weights-Audited" to avoid legal signal implication? Legal should help craft the badge wording.
- How often do we re-run the eval suites and latency tests? Nightly is expensive; weekly might be acceptable. Need infra estimate.
- Probe privacy: ensure samples from customer probes aren’t used for internal evals unless opted-in.

Next steps (who does what):
- PMM (Maya): draft catalog card templates and short explainer page (2 weeks).
- Eng (Amit): prototype health snapshot runner and baseline latency harness (3 sprints).
- SE (Liam): design the 5-prompt probe templates and field test with 3 pilot customers (4 weeks).
- Legal (Sana): review badge wording and audit checklist (2 weeks).

Appendix / quick reference (links to artifacts):
- Confluence: MC-4521 (health spec) — linked above.
- GitHub: proto harness PR — linked above.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep messaging engineering-first; avoid hype words like "best" or "state-of-the-art" in catalog cards.
- Prioritize a clear cost band visualization — PMs consistently ask for a one-glance tradeoff view.
- If we add a safety badge, make sure it is scope-limited and points at tests run.

End of draft.

(If this looks good, I will convert into a one-pager for the launch briefing and a short doc for the docs site explaining the math behind p95 extrapolations.)
